claims.text: What the strip looks like The changes usually start at the T wave and move forward along the trace: first the T wave, then the P wave and PR interval, then the QRS (widening and conduction blocks).
claims.quote: An easy way to remember the usual order of ECG changes seen is by following the ECG trace logically – effects begin on the T wave and move forwards to the P wave / PR interval, and subsequently to the QRS complex with QRS widening and conduction blocks.

claims.text: Aspects (abnormal in red) T waves (first): peaked, narrow-based (early; K ~5.5–6.5)
claims.quote: 1. Peaked, narrow-based T waves (early; K ~5.5–6.5)

claims.text: P wave and PR (next): P wave flattening and PR prolongation
claims.quote: 2. P wave flattening and PR prolongation

claims.text: QRS (then): widening
claims.quote: 3. QRS widening

claims.text: Late: QRS merges with the T wave → “sine wave” (imminent arrest)
claims.quote: 4. Merging of QRS with T → "sine wave" (imminent arrest)

claims.text: End: asystole or VF
claims.quote: 5. Asystole or VF

claims.text: QT: shortened, alongside a longer PR, as conduction slows
claims.quote: Slowing of conduction is characterized by an increased PR interval and shortening of the QT interval.

claims.text: Rate and rhythm: bradyarrhythmias — sinus bradycardia, high-grade AV block with slow junctional and ventricular escape rhythms, slow AF
claims.quote: Bradyarrhythmias: sinus bradycardia, high-grade AV block with slow junctional and ventricular escape rhythms, slow AF

claims.text: Conduction: bundle branch or fascicular blocks
claims.quote: Conduction blocks (bundle branch block, fascicular blocks)

claims.text: Caution: the potassium level may not correlate closely with the ECG — a patient with a relatively normal ECG can still have a sudden hyperkalemic cardiac arrest
claims.quote: Note: Serum potassium level may not correlate closely with ECG changes. Patients with a relatively normal ECG can suffer sudden hyperkalaemia cardiac arrest.

claims.text: Causes (mechanism and diagnoses) Mechanism: raised extracellular potassium reduces myocardial excitability, depressing both pacemaking and conducting tissue
claims.quote: Increased extracellular potassium reduces myocardial excitability, with depression of both pacemaking and conducting tissues.

claims.text: Definition and cause: serum potassium > 5.5 mEq/L, usually from decreased renal potassium excretion or abnormal movement of potassium out of cells; usually several factors contribute at once
claims.quote: Hyperkalemia is a serum potassium concentration > 5.5 mEq/L (> 5.5 mmol/L), usually resulting from decreased renal potassium excretion or abnormal movement of potassium out of cells. There are usually several simultaneous contributing factors

claims.text: Common causes: potassium-retaining medications, renal insufficiency, adrenal insufficiency, and cell breakdown (e.g., rhabdomyolysis, burns, bleeding into soft tissue or the GI tract)
claims.quote: Common causes of hyperkalemia include potassium-retaining medications, renal insufficiency, adrenal insufficiency, and disorders involving cellular breakdown (eg, rhabdomyolysis, burns, bleeding into soft tissue or the gastrointestinal tract).

claims.text: Suspect it in any patient with a new bradyarrhythmia or AV block, especially in renal failure, on hemodialysis, or taking any combination of ACE inhibitors, potassium-sparing diuretics and potassium supplements
claims.quote: Suspect hyperkalaemia in any patient with a new bradyarrhythmia or AV block, especially patients with renal failure, on haemodialysis, or taking any combination of ACE inhibitors, potassium-sparing diuretics and potassium supplements.

claims.text: Pseudohyperkalemia: most often from hemolysis of the blood sample
claims.quote: Pseudohyperkalemia is most often caused by hemolysis of red blood cells in a blood sample.

claims.text: Symptoms Usually asymptomatic until cardiac toxicity develops, although some patients have weakness
claims.quote: Hyperkalemia is usually asymptomatic until cardiac toxicity develops, although some patients have weakness.

claims.text: Flaccid paralysis occasionally occurs
claims.quote: Although flaccid paralysis occasionally occurs, hyperkalemia is usually asymptomatic until cardiac arrhythmias develop.

claims.text: Treatment Loss of P waves or a wide QRS: IV calcium plus insulin and glucose — 10 to 20 mL of 10% calcium gluconate (or 5 to 10 mL of 22% calcium gluceptate) IV over 5 to 10 minutes
claims.quote: If ECG changes include the loss of P-wave or widening of the QRS complex, treatment with IV calcium as well as insulin and glucose is indicated; 10 to 20 mL of 10% calcium gluconate (or 5 to 10 mL of 22% calcium gluceptate) is given IV over 5 to 10 minutes.

claims.text: Sine wave or asystole: calcium gluconate may be given more rapidly (5 to 10 mL IV over 2 minutes)
claims.quote: If the ECG shows a sine wave pattern or asystole, calcium gluconate may be given more rapidly (5 to 10 mL IV over 2 minutes).

claims.text: Calcium antagonizes the effect of hyperkalemia on cardiac muscle
claims.quote: Calcium antagonizes the effect of hyperkalemia on cardiac muscle.

claims.text: Calcium works within minutes but lasts only 20 to 30 minutes — it is a temporizing measure while other treatments or hemodialysis take effect, and may need repeating
claims.quote: The benefits of calcium occur within minutes but last only 20 to 30 minutes. Calcium infusion is a temporizing measure while awaiting the effects of other treatments or initiation of hemodialysis and may need to be repeated.

claims.text: Give calcium with caution to patients taking digoxin (risk of precipitating hypokalemia-related arrhythmias)
claims.quote: Calcium should be given with caution to patients taking digoxin because of the risk of precipitating hypokalemia-related arrhythmias.

claims.text: Potassium > 6.5 mEq/L: more aggressive therapy — regular insulin 5 to 10 units IV, followed immediately by (or given with) a rapid infusion of 50 mL of 50% glucose, then 10% dextrose at 50 mL/hour to prevent hypoglycemia
claims.quote: If serum potassium is > 6.5 mEq/L (> 6.5 mmol/L), more aggressive therapy is required. Administration of regular insulin 5 to 10 units IV is followed immediately by or administered simultaneously with rapid infusion of 50 mL 50% glucose. Infusion of 10% dextrose in water should follow at 50 mL/hour to prevent hypoglycemia.

claims.text: Adjunct: a high-dose inhaled beta 2-agonist (e.g., albuterol 10 to 20 mg over 10 minutes) may help; beta 2-agonists are contraindicated in unstable angina or acute MI
claims.quote: A high-dose beta 2-agonist, such as albuterol 10 to 20 mg inhaled over 10 minutes (5 mg/mL concentration), can lower serum potassium by 0.5 to 1.5 mEq/L (0.5 to 1.5 mmol/L) and may be a helpful adjunct. The peak effect occurs in 90 minutes. However, beta 2-agonists are contraindicated in patients with unstable angina or acute myocardial infarction.

claims.text: Hemodialysis: start promptly when emergency medical treatment is ineffective, especially with severe chronic kidney disease and/or acute kidney injury
claims.quote: Hemodialysis should be instituted promptly when emergency medical treatment is ineffective especially in patients with severe chronic kidney disease and/or acute kidney injury.

claims.text: Mild (potassium < 6 mEq/L, no ECG changes): may respond to less potassium intake or stopping potassium-raising medications; adding a loop diuretic helps if the patient is not volume depleted
claims.quote: Patients with serum potassium < 6 mEq/L (< 6 mmol/L) and no ECG abnormalities may respond to diminished potassium intake or stopping potassium-elevating medications. The addition of a loop diuretic enhances renal potassium excretion as long as volume depletion is not present.

claims.text: Mild: sodium polystyrene sulfonate, patiromer, or sodium zirconium cyclosilicate
claims.quote: Give sodium polystyrene sulfonate, patiromer, or sodium zirconium cyclosilicate for mild hyperkalemia.

claims.text: Patiromer and sodium zirconium silicate are not recommended as emergency treatment (delayed onset)
claims.quote: Patiromer and sodium zirconium silicate are not recommended for use as an emergency treatment to acutely lower potassium because of these medications' delayed onset of action.

notes.issue: "sodium zirconium" is not a drug name; the quote says "sodium zirconium silicate"
